title: Type Hints
description: Adding optional static type annotations to variables and functions, and the tools that check them.
objectives: Add type hints to variables and function signatures
Use Optional and Union to express more complex types
Understand the benefits and limitations of type hints

content.heading: Annotating Variables and Functions
content.body: Python remains dynamically typed at runtime, but since Python 3.5 it supports optional type hints (also called type annotations) — a way to document, and let external tools check, what type a variable, parameter, or return value is expected to be, without the interpreter enforcing it at runtime. A variable annotation looks like age: int = 21. A function annotation looks like def greet(name: str) -> str:, declaring name should be a str and the function returns a str. These hints are purely informational to the Python interpreter itself; nothing stops you from passing the 'wrong' type at runtime — enforcement comes from separate static type checkers.

content.heading: Optional, Union, and Generic Collections
content.body:
Optional[X] (from the typing module, or the newer X | None syntax in Python 3.10+) means 'a value of type X, or None' — commonly used for parameters or return values that might be absent. Union[X, Y] (or X | Y) means 'either type X or type Y'. Generic collection types express what's inside a container: list[int] is a list whose elements are all expected to be int, dict[str, float] a dict mapping strings to floats (in Python 3.9+, the built-in list/dict/etc. can be parameterized directly; older code uses typing.List, typing.Dict).

The main benefit of type hints is tooling: editors can offer better autocomplete, and static type checkers like mypy can catch a whole class of type-related bugs before the code even runs, without any runtime cost. The main limitation is exactly that they are not enforced by the Python interpreter itself — a type-hinted function will still happily accept the 'wrong' type at runtime unless a separate checker is run as part of your workflow.

content.explanation: Optional[str] documents that find_user might return None. list[float] and dict[str, int] describe the expected element/key/value types of the collections — none of this is checked at runtime by Python itself.

keyPoints: Type hints (x: int, def f(x: int) -> str:) are optional and not enforced by the Python runtime
Optional[X] means X or None; Union[X, Y] (or X | Y) means either type
list[int], dict[str, float], etc. express the expected contents of a collection
Static type checkers (like mypy) are what actually catch type mismatches — hints alone are just documentation
commonMistakes: Believing a type hint actually prevents the wrong type from being passed at runtime
Forgetting Optional[X] when a function can genuinely return None
Mixing old-style typing.List/typing.Dict and new-style list/dict hints inconsistently across a codebase without a version reason
